article_title: Linking Disparate Strands: A Critical Review of the Relationship Between Creativity and Education
citation: Bruce S. Rawlings & Sarah J. Cutting. (2024). Linking Disparate Strands: A Critical Review of the Relationship Between Creativity and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09973-z
title: Divergent and convergent thinking as the two core components of creativity used to organize the education–creativity debate
description: The review organizes its synthesis around a two-component account of creativity as "the ability to generate novel and useful ideas", comprising "divergent thinking—the capacity to produce multiple novel ideas, solutions or possibilities" and "convergent thinking—homing in on single, correct solutions from a range of options". Divergent thinking involves fluent, original, flexible and elaborate production; convergent thinking requires logical thinking, accuracy, precision and deduction to evaluate and select optimal solutions. Both are required for creativity, yet divergent thinking has received far more scientific focus and is often used as a proxy for overall creative ability.
requirements: Both divergent and convergent thinking are required for creativity; the former produces novel ideas and the latter evaluates them to optimise value
constraints: The review restricts its scope to divergent and convergent thinking because they are the most widely used creativity measures in education, setting aside debates over the validity and reliability of other creativity measures
examples: The PISA 2022 Assessment and Analytical Framework breaks creative thinking into generating diverse ideas, generating creative ideas, and evaluating and improving ideas—facets the review says are captured by both divergent and convergent thinking
key_sources: Bruce S. Rawlings & Sarah J. Cutting. (2024). Linking Disparate Strands: A Critical Review of the Relationship Between Creativity and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09973-z

article_title: Data-driven unsupervised clustering of online learner behaviour
citation: Peach, R. L., Yaliraki, S. N., Lefevre, D. and Barahona, M. (2019). Data-driven unsupervised clustering of online learner behaviour. npj Science of Learning 4:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0054-0
title: DTW-kernel, RMST-sparsified similarity graph with Markov Stability multiscale clustering of learner time-series
description: A three-stage unsupervised framework for analysing online learner temporal behaviour. A dynamic time warping kernel computes pairwise similarity between raw time-series: "Our method uses a dynamic time warping similarity kernel to generate a sparsified similarity graph between learners, to which we apply a multiscale graph partitioning algorithm". RMST sparsification retains strong, globally relevant edges; Markov Stability scans Markov time to find robust partitions at all resolutions without pre-imposing cluster number or type, yielding a quasi-hierarchy from 10 down to 2 clusters that the analyst can choose from.
requirements: Time-stamped interaction data (task completions or page clicks) for each learner; robustness is assessed via low VI(t) dips and persistent VI(t,t') plateaus across scales.
constraints: Temporal behaviours do not fully account for learner performance, and the authors state it is not intended as a diagnostic tool but for exploration, aid, intervention and course design.
target_learning_goals: identifying temporal engagement behaviours (distributed vs massed vs sporadic learning)
flagging learners at risk of low performance for aid and intervention
examples: Applied to 81 learners over six online courses of a part-time management degree, yielding robust 10-, 6- and 2-cluster partitions with 'Early Birds', 'On time', 'Low Engagers', 'Crammers' and sporadic outliers.
key_sources: Peach, R. L., Yaliraki, S. N., Lefevre, D. and Barahona, M. (2019). Data-driven unsupervised clustering of online learner behaviour. npj Science of Learning 4:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0054-0

article_title: Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Joelle Fingerhut, & Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 37(4), 239–250. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076
title: Meta-analytic dataset of 46 single-case experimental design studies of DTT training (224 participants)
description: The compiled corpus for this meta-analysis: 46 SCED studies of trainings for DTT implementation fidelity, selected via PRISMA procedures from four databases plus an ancestry search, with raw data extracted using WebPlot Digitizer 2.0. The article reports that "The number of participants across all 46 studies was 224" and that "A total of 130 (58%) participants received BST as their training." Studies met WWC (2020) standards with or without reservations, and interobserver agreement for coding was 100% on a 30% subset.
requirements: Included studies needed DTT fidelity directly observed on a percentage scale, an SCED with three demonstrations of intervention effectiveness, and WWC-compliant data points per phase
constraints: Studies pairing DTT training with training for another teaching method were excluded to avoid confounding
Duplicate data (e.g., dissertations later published) were excluded
target_learners: Special education teachers, paraprofessionals, parents, clinicians, and other DTT implementers across school, clinic, university, and home settings
target_learning_goals: Implementing discrete trial training with fidelity
examples: Table 1 lists 13 training combinations across studies and participants, with complete BST the most common (20 studies, 76 participants).
key_sources: Joelle Fingerhut, & Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 37(4), 239–250. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076

article_title: Effect of massed versus distributed preclinical training on subgingival instrumentation skill across the preclinical-to-clinical transition.
citation: Glevitzky, L., Cyris, M., Sutor, S., Springer, C., Kahl, M., Mekhemar, M., Sälzer, S. & Graetz, C. (2026). Effect of massed versus distributed preclinical training on subgingival instrumentation skill across the preclinical-to-clinical transition. Scientific Reports 16, 23355. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62235-6
title: Digitised training programme (DTP) for preclinical subgingival instrumentation
description: The DTP is the shared digitised preclinical training programme used as the constant in both schedules: it comprises "the same theoretical introduction, digital self-learning material (DTP), instruments, supervision key (one board-certified periodontist per ten students) and calibration of application pressure (3–5 N for GRA, <1 N for AIR)". Previous work by the group found the digitised programme superior to the former conventional programme and enables high cleaning efficacies with both instrument types.
requirements: Mandatory attendance and completion of the full 9 h of guided practice; supervision at one board-certified periodontist per ten students with calibrated application pressure.
constraints: The article evaluates the DTP only in an in vitro manikin-based model with simulated biofilm and calculus.
target_learning_goals: subgingival instrumentation with Gracey curettes and sonic scalers
examples: Students instrumented six test teeth on periodontitis manikins coated with fluorescent varnish simulating biofilm and varnish simulating calculus.
key_sources: Glevitzky, L., Cyris, M., Sutor, S., Springer, C., Kahl, M., Mekhemar, M., Sälzer, S. & Graetz, C. (2026). Effect of massed versus distributed preclinical training on subgingival instrumentation skill across the preclinical-to-clinical transition. Scientific Reports 16, 23355. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62235-6
